findings.title: A GET request changes a user's notification state
findings.body: The `unsubscribe` action is exposed as a GET route and explicitly skips the XHR/CSRF protection, but it writes `TopicUser.notification_level`. Any third-party page can cause a logged-in user's browser to request a known `/t/<slug>/<id>/unsubscribe` URL (for example via an image), muting or changing that user's topic notifications without consent. Link scanners and prefetchers can also trigger the mutation. Make the state change a CSRF-protected non-GET request, or use a purpose-bound signed unsubscribe token that is safe to consume from an email link.

findings.title: The unsubscribe link does not reliably unsubscribe watched/tracked users
findings.body: For notification levels above `regular`, following the email's “stop receiving notifications” link changes the level only to `regular`, not `muted`. Regular users can still receive topic notifications such as replies or mentions, so the link's stated result is not achieved. It also makes the outcome dependent on the current level: a second invocation changes regular to muted, while an initial invocation for a watcher does not. Set the intended unsubscribed state directly (normally `muted`) so the operation is idempotent.

findings.title: Directly saving TopicUser bypasses notification-change bookkeeping
findings.body: This action mutates and saves the TopicUser row directly instead of using `TopicUser.change`, which is the established path for notification-level changes. As a result it does not set `notifications_changed_at`, does not mark `notifications_reason_id` as `user_changed`, and does not publish the MessageBus notification-level update. In particular, a row whose reason remains nil may subsequently be auto-promoted back to tracking by `update_last_read`, undoing the unsubscribe; active clients can also continue to display stale notification state. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user, topic_id, notification_level: ...)` rather than assigning and saving the record.
